title: Bean Stew with Smoked Fish
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: The earlier, plainer version — no plantain, no name, a twenty-minute simmer and a printed question mark where the chilli quantity should be.
longDesc: Two years before she published red red, the same author published this: a cup of dried cowpeas washed, soaked and cooked, a medium onion, an eight-ounce tin of tomato sauce, half a pound of smoked fish, a quarter to a third of a cup of palm oil and half a teaspoon of salt, simmered approximately twenty minutes. The phrase red red does not appear anywhere in it, and there is no fried plantain. It is the same stew without the elements that make it red red — and it carries a printed question mark where the chilli quantity should be, which is reproduced rather than filled in.
ingredients: 1 cup dried cowpeas, washed, soaked and cooked
Dried red pepper — the source prints '1/8 - ? tsp'. See the note.
steps: Wash and soak the cowpeas, then cook them until tender.
Add the tomato sauce and the palm oil.
Add the smoked fish and the dried red pepper.
Season with the salt and serve.
chefTips: Twenty minutes here against about ten in her later red red. The longer simmer gives a deeper, more melded stew.
Her storage note is the best reason to make this version: it freezes well, and it tastes even better the next day.
The chilli quantity is genuinely missing — the source prints a question mark. Start at an eighth of a teaspoon and go up.
A quarter to a third of a cup of palm oil, slightly less than the later version's third of a cup. Leaner.
Cowpeas and black-eyed peas are the same family and the two recipes use the two names interchangeably.
No plantain in this version, which makes it a stew rather than a plate. If you want red red, add fried plantain and you have essentially GHA069.
Soak properly rather than quick-boiling. This version assumes a conventional soak.
commonMistakes: Guessing high on the missing chilli quantity.
Eating it the day it is made, when it is better the next.
Using a refined oil instead of palm oil.
Expecting it to be red red without the plantain.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #18: Bean Stew w/smoked fish', betumiblog.blogspot.com, 13 October 2009. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 10:45 AM'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS). NO YIELD is printed.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 cup dried cowpeas (a cup of dried cowpeas washed, soaked and cooked); 1 medium onion; 8-oz can tomato sauce; 1/2 pound smoked fish; about 1/4-1/3 cup palm oil; 1/2 t salt; '1/8 - ? t dried red pepper'.

A PRINTED QUESTION MARK, reproduced and NOT filled in: the chilli quantity reads '1/8 - ? t dried red pepper'. The question mark is in the source. No upper figure has been invented; the ingredient list above reproduces the printed form with a pointer to this note.
STORAGE NOTE, verbatim: 'it freezes well, it tastes even better the next day'.

THE NAME IS ABSENT: the phrase 'red red' DOES NOT APPEAR anywhere in this post, which is why it is published as bean stew rather than as a version of red red. Her red red post came two years later (GHA069).

THE DISAGREEMENT WITH HER LATER VERSION, unreconciled: this one uses 1/4-1/3 cup palm oil and simmers about 20 minutes; the later red red uses 1/3 cup and simmers about 10 minutes, and adds fried plantain. Both are published as printed.
NO DONENESS CUE beyond the twenty-minute simmer. The beans are cooked separately before they go in.
ON COWPEAS: the same legume family as black-eyed peas, and the two names are used interchangeably across her two posts.
storage: 4 days refrigerated, and it freezes well — her own note. Better the next day.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas are high in plant protein, folate, iron and soluble fibre.
Red palm oil provides provitamin-A carotenoids.
Smoked fish adds omega-3 fats and iodine.
culturalNote: Seeing a cook publish the plain stew first and the named, plantain-accompanied version two years later is a small record of how a dish gets recognised — the stew was always there, and red red is what it becomes when you put the plantain beside it and give it a name.
